qs.q: A pregnant woman presents with a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated lesion on her gingiva that bleeds easily. If this lesion is a pyogenic granuloma, what is the most likely treatment?
o: Radical excision of the underlying bone
Systemic antibiotic therapy for Bartonella henselae
Observation, as it will regress spontaneously by age 7
qs.e: Pyogenic granulomas are treated with curettage and cautery. They do not regress by age 7 (that is for juvenile hemangiomas) and are not caused by Bartonella in this context.

faq.a: No, it is a vascular lesion; the name is a misnomer.
Very rarely; malignant transformation is not a common concern.
In many settings, clinical diagnosis and excision are acceptable; send a sample to a regional lab if possible.
faq.q: What if I cannot do a biopsy?

exam: What is the most likely cause of a rapidly growing red gingival mass in a pregnant woman? — Hormonal changes (estrogen/progesterone) and local trauma.
Which investigation confirms the diagnosis? — Excision with histology showing lobular capillary proliferation.
What is the first step in management if the lesion bleeds profusely? — Apply direct pressure and consider cautery or excision.
How would you differentiate it from peripheral ossifying fibroma? — Ossifying fibroma is firm, may calcify, and is less vascular.
Why are topical steroids used after excision? — To reduce residual inflammation and bleeding.
What red flag would prompt urgent referral? — Uncontrolled bleeding or rapid growth >2 cm.
ai.title: Pyogenic Granuloma
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A rapidly growing, vascular pedunculated lesion, often on gingiva or skin, that bleeds easily. It is a lobular capillary hemangioma, not an infectious granuloma. Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by excision and histology.

b: Common on gingiva, fingers, lips, oral mucosa
sections.p: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, lobular capillary hemangioma that presents as a red, friable, pedunculated mass. It is not a true granuloma and is not caused by infection. Diagnosis is mainly clinical; definitive confirmation requires excision and histology showing lobular aggregates of capillaries with surrounding inflammatory cells.
Severity is usually graded by size and bleeding tendency. There is no formal staging system, but lesions >2 cm or with uncontrolled bleeding are considered high‑risk for morbidity.

t.b: If yes, consider urgent excision or cautery

sections.p: The main drivers are local trauma, hormonal changes (especially pregnancy), and chronic irritation. In low‑resource settings, infections such as HIV or chronic oral infections may act as co‑factors.

t.b: Pregnancy increases risk; consider pregnancy‑related management

sections.p: Patients report a rapidly enlarging, red, sometimes ulcerated mass that bleeds on touch. In children it may appear on the gingiva; in adults it can be on fingers or lips.
Routine investigations are usually unnecessary. Excision provides both diagnosis and treatment. In resource‑limited settings, a simple biopsy is sufficient.

t.b: Lobular capillary proliferation with inflammatory infiltrate confirms pyogenic granuloma

sections.p: Complications include significant bleeding, infection, and, rarely, malignant transformation (very uncommon). Red flags are uncontrolled bleeding, rapid enlargement, or ulceration with pain.

t.b: Apply direct pressure, consider cautery or excision

sections.p: First treat the underlying cause (remove irritants, manage pregnancy). Definitive treatment is surgical excision with cautery or laser. Topical steroids may be used for residual lesions.

t.b: It removes the lesion and reduces recurrence

sections.p: After excision, monitor for recurrence, especially if trauma persists. Prevent recurrence by good oral hygiene, avoiding trauma, and managing pregnancy hormones.
Differential includes peripheral ossifying fibroma, squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, and Kaposi sarcoma.

b: Limited biopsy may miss lobular pattern
sections.p: Histology may show inflammatory infiltrate that can be mistaken for infection. In low‑resource settings, limited pathology may miss subtle features.
